newsitem.title: USA: People care passionately about hating junk E-mail.
newsitem.headline: People care passionately about hating junk E-mail.

text.p: - Junk e-mail, how do I hate thee? Let me count the ways.
I hate thee to the depth of my e-mailbox, which you fill with unwanted clutter o'er the day.
I hate thee purely, for bearing a false "sender" name, making it impossible to purge myself from thy wretched list.
I hate thee passionately, inflaming an irresistible urge to curse my otherwise beloved PC.
People hate junk e-mail.
No, they don't just hate it. They despise it, detest it, abhor it, complain about it and downright can't stand it.
"In snail mail, the sender pays. In junk e-mail, the receiver pays. NOT FAIR NOT FAIR NOT FAIR," wrote one America Online subscriber, responding to an informal online survey about junk e-mail.
"I hold the Internet as sacred, and see junk e-mail as spoiling it," wrote Paul Chamberlain, an IBM Internet division employee, also responding to the survey.
However much people decry them, though, unsolicited electronic advertisements have become a staple of digital life, right up there with e-mail addresses and Web site URLs.

Junk e-mail -- direct marketers refer to it as "bulk e-mail" -- comes in many flavors, including come ons for get-rich quick schemes, low-priced Internet access providers, chain letters, online psychics, and on and on.

The growing spate of junk e-mail has led to legal tussles, including the ongoing courtroom battle between America Online and Cyber Promotions Inc., of Philadelphia. The central issue: whether Cyber Promotions has the legal right to send junk e-mail to AOL subscribers, or whether AOL can legally block it. The lawsuits are pending.

Meanwhile, there's not much people can do up front to prevent their addresses from ending up on one or another junk e-mail list, short of using anonymous remailers to mask the origin of every message they send.

"All they have to do is look at the (Usenet) newsgroups I've posted to, and there it is," wrote J. Miller, responding to the survey. "If that doesn't work, they just go to my Internet service provider and find out from there. I don't mind getting e-mail that's intended as advertisements, but when I get things for KKK sign ups, phone sex lines and just plain harassing mail, that is an invasion of my dignity."

Once they get it, people have different ways of dealing with unwanted mail. Some delete messages unread. Others use e-mail software to permanently block messages from addresses they know to be bad news.

"I'm close to the point where I'm going to start filtering out all mail that comes from entire domains," wrote Internet user Al Crawford. "I can see the day when my mail filter deletes everything except mail that contains some special key word in the subject line that only friends will know."
Others take a more emotional tack.

"I respond in a nasty way to the sender, enclosing the entire note," wrote Internet user James Marshall. "I also take note of who the company is, and make a point to boycott them entirely, and encourage all my friends to do so."
Some people find junk e-mail so aggravating, they're ready to sue, or pass laws banning it.

"I work at a state university and since the university networks are used to deliver my mail, basically junk e-mailers are spending state funds to get their mail to me. It will be interesting if our lawyers can turn this around to make (a) case against them," wrote Stew Crawford-Hines, from Colorado State University.
"I'd like to see the same level of penalties the feds provide for repeat offenders in telephone solicitations," wrote Paul Canniff.

Expanding federal junk-fax laws to cover junk e-mail could have unintended results, according to net activists. Laws proposing that people should receive only communications they ask for could violate the First Amendment, and preclude anyone receiving anything they didn't already know about, including alerts about fast-moving legislation or net dangers, even a letter from a long-lost friend, activists said.
A minority of Internet users aren't bothered by unexpected mail, no matter how junky.
"I get about 75 to 100 e-mails a day and so far none of them are junk mail. To me there is no issue," wrote E. Denson, responding to the poll.
In fact, a small -- very small -- slice of the wired populace likes it.

"The debate of junk e-mail is much ado about nothing," wrote James Anderson. "I enjoy all of my e-mail correspondence. I always have the option of filtering or deleting. I do like (Microsoft Chairman) Bill Gates' idea of payment for reading e-mail advertisements. The truth is I would read anything for a fee if I had the time."
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
